body.statement: Fix \(m\) and \(p\). The cohort-mean PPML-imputation estimator is semiparametrically efficient for \(\theta_{\mathrm{PTT}}\) at every law \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\) satisfying \(\mathbb E_PY=m\) if and only if \(q=0\); when \(q>0\), its efficient covariance laws are exactly \(\mathcal L(m)\cap\ker(\mathcal L_m)\), where \(\mathcal L_m:\mathcal A_{\Sigma}\to\mathbb R^q\) has rank \(q\), and \(\|b_{\mathrm{cyc}}\|_2^2/\lambda_{\max}(K)\le\Gamma\le\|b_{\mathrm{cyc}}\|_2^2/\lambda_{\min}(K)\). This strictly sharpens Ciani and Fisher's printed-page-7, Section 3.1 observation and Appendix B simulation evidence that PPML may fail to be most efficient by giving necessity, sufficiency, and codimension for the stated cohort-mean estimator.
body.justification: This is the topology-level kernel: cycles are necessary and sufficient for covariance laws on which feasible precision improvement exists.
body.gap: Ciani and Fisher (2019, printed page 7, Section 3.1) state that PPML may fail to be the most efficient estimator, with the corresponding efficiency-loss simulations in Appendix B; Moreau--Kastler (2025, equations 3.13--3.14) and Wooldridge (2023, Sections 2--3) study distinct individual-level imputation procedures. None gives an acyclic if-and-only-if frontier or an exact codimension count for the cohort-mean rank-one estimator.
body.consumer: The theorem tells analysts in the Nagengast--Yotov and Menkhoff--Miethe settings exactly when the transparent cohort-mean PPML benchmark is universally precision-optimal before moving to richer individual-level specifications.
